lessons.title: Inspecting animals and reporting abnormal behaviour
lessons.html:
Daily health checks

A good stockman checks the animals every day. The aim is to find sick or injured animals early, when treatment works best and costs less. Check animals at the same time each day, for example when they come to the water trough or into the kraal.

What to check

Body partHealthyAbnormal
BehaviourAlert, stays with the group, eatsDull, alone, not eating, restless, kicking at belly
Eyes and noseBright eyes, clean moist noseRunny or cloudy eyes, thick nose discharge
BreathingSlow and quiet at restFast, noisy, coughing, mouth open
Skin and coatSmooth, shiny, clean woolHair loss, wounds, heavy ticks, lumps
Legs and feetWalks evenlyLimping, swollen joints, smelly hooves
Dung and urineNormal colour and firmnessVery runny, bloody, no dung, red urine
UdderSoft, evenHot, hard, swollen, abnormal milk

Looking at the inner eyelid

In sheep and goats, pale pink or white inner eyelids can mean anaemia, often caused by wireworm. Many farms use a colour chart for this check. Report pale animals to your supervisor.

Reporting

Write down the animal's tag number, the camp, the date and time, and exactly what you saw. Report the same day. Report at once if you see bloat, an animal that cannot stand, heavy bleeding, difficult birth or several animals dead or sick at the same time. These may be emergencies or signs of a serious disease.

lessons.title: Moving and restraining animals for procedures
lessons.html:
Planning the work

Basic procedures such as dosing, injecting, tagging or checking feet need animals to be moved and restrained. At this level you help to supervise this work, so you must make sure it is done safely and humanely.

Before you start

  • Check the kraal, race and crush: no broken poles, sharp wire or loose gates.
  • Make sure there are enough workers and that each person knows their job.
  • Have the equipment ready before the animals come in.
  • Work in the cool part of the day in summer.

Moving animals

Use the animals' flight zone and herd instinct. Work quietly from behind and to the side. Use flags or boards. Move small groups into the race so animals do not pile up. Do not let workers shout, hit or use sticks.

Restraint

  • Cattle: in the crush with the head clamp and back bar closed. A halter can be used for the head.
  • Sheep and goats: in a small pen or race. Catch a sheep by the jaw and flank, or set it on its rump for foot work. Never lift by the wool.
  • Pigs: in a small pen with a pig board.

Release animals as soon as the procedure is done. Restraint must be no tighter or longer than needed. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty an offence.

Safety

Never stand directly behind cattle or in the space between an animal and a wall. Keep hands out of the crush when the animal is moving. Watch new or young workers closely.

lessons.title: Basic procedures and biosecurity
lessons.html:
Basic procedures under supervision

At this level you carry out basic procedures under full supervision of the farm manager or vet. Always follow the instructions and the product label.

  • Dosing: use the right product and the right dose for the animal's weight, as on the label. Calibrate the dosing gun before you start. Place the nozzle over the tongue gently so the animal does not choke.
  • Injecting: use clean, sharp needles. Inject in the place shown on the label, usually the neck, to avoid damage to valuable meat cuts.
  • Tick control: spray, pour-on or dip as instructed.
  • Wound care: clean the wound and apply the product given by the supervisor.

Record every treatment: animal number, product, dose, date and who gave it. Note the withdrawal period on the label: the animal may not be slaughtered and its milk may not be sold before that time is over. Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling remedies registered under Act 36 of 1947.

Basic biosecurity

Biosecurity means stopping disease from coming onto the farm and from spreading on the farm.

  • Keep new or bought animals apart (quarantine) before they join the herd, for the time your vet advises.
  • Keep sick animals in a sick pen away from healthy ones.
  • Control visitors and vehicles. Use foot baths where provided.
  • Clean and disinfect equipment such as needles, dosing guns and hoof knives.
  • Do not share equipment with neighbours without cleaning it.
  • Dispose of dead animals as the supervisor instructs. Do not open carcasses of animals that died suddenly.
  • Report suspected notifiable diseases. The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 requires this.

Key points

  • Check animals daily and report abnormal signs the same day.
  • Pale inner eyelids in sheep and goats can mean wireworm anaemia.
  • Restrain animals safely and humanely, and release them quickly.
  • Follow the label for dose and withdrawal period, and record every treatment.
  • Quarantine new animals, isolate sick animals and clean equipment.
